iconicAnchor.creatorOrTradition: New Mexican tinwork and devotional arts
iconicAnchor.whyCanonical: The Smithsonian object joins tin and wood craft, devotional imagery, named makers, regional history, and cultural affirmation in one clearly documented nicho.

sources.title: El Gran Poder de Dios Niche
supports: A documented New Mexican nicho combines tinwork, wood, paint, glass, devotional imagery, named artists, and cultural affirmation.

sources.title: Santos and Ofrendas: Ten Highlights of Latinx Art at the Smithsonian
supports: New Mexican retablo practice uses saturated outlined sacred imagery within a living santero tradition shaped by Mexican and Southwest cultural histories.

bundledReferenceRationale: Excellent replacement lead with genuinely distinct process support. The lead independently teaches the complete hojalata object, reflective worked-tin construction, intimate shrine scale, and painted narrative center at card scale. The support adds visible hand-punching, repoussé work, cutting, joining, tools, offcuts, and assembly. Together they are materially specific, culturally framed, non-redundant, and clearly separated from adjacent folk-vernacular styles. The independently approved lead is assets/refs/mexican-tinwork/reference-01.jpg. Distinct supporting role: Complementary material-process exemplar; teaches construction without duplicating the complete-object lead.

culturalContext.note: Name the specific retablo, nicho, santero, Mexican, or New Mexican context and preserve maker, devotional, and community meaning. Do not extract saints, votive narratives, or milagro-like symbols as generic Southwestern decoration. For contemporary use, favor commissioned work, accurate attribution, and non-sacred structural cues when cultural participation is absent.
